questions.prompt: Which of the following circuits, driven by a source \(v_{s}(t)\) with output \(v_{o}(t)\), is an LTI system?
options: A resistor in series with a diode, output across the diode
A network of fixed resistors, capacitors, inductors and a linear dependent source
A resistor in series with a capacitor whose value varies as \(C(t)=C_{0}(1+0.2\cos(2\pi\cdot 1\ \mathrm{kHz}\cdot t))\), output across C
A resistor whose value grows with time as \(R(t)=R_{0}(1+0.1t)\), with a fixed capacitor, output across C
questions.explanation:
LTI circuits are built from fixed (constant-value) linear elements: R, L, C, mutual inductors, and linear dependent sources.
• The diode has an exponential I–V curve, so the circuit is nonlinear.
• A capacitor whose value changes in time is linear but time-VARYING (the circuit behaves differently depending on when the input arrives).
• A resistor drifting with time is likewise linear but time-varying.
Only the fixed-element network satisfies both properties.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter is at rest. A constant input of height \(V_s\) turns on at time \(t_0\), not at time 0. Order the reasoning for the output after \(t_0\).
questions.explanation: A time-invariant circuit does not care that the clock read 0 at some earlier moment. The transient starts when the input changes. Using \(t\) rather than \(t-t_0\) in the exponent pretends the step happened at 0, so the output would already have risen by \(t_0\). The final value is still the input, because the capacitor current dies out.
steps: Before \(t_0\) the input is still 0, so the output stays 0.
After \(t_0\) the final value is \(V_s\). The output starts from the 0 left by the previous step.
Measure the exponent from the switching instant that ended that rest, so the elapsed time is \(t - t_0\).
For \(t > t_0\), write \(v_o(t) = V_s\left(1 - e^{-(t - t_0)/\tau}\right)\), using the final value and the elapsed time from the previous steps.

questions.prompt: Preview of open-circuit time constants. A later skill finds a circuit's time constant as \(\tau=R_{\mathrm{th}}\cdot C\), where \(R_{\mathrm{th}}\) is the resistance seen by the capacitor with the independent sources turned off. A node has \(C=2\ \mathrm{nF}\), with 1 kΩ and 4 kΩ resistors connecting it to the source and to ground (the source is an ideal voltage source). After a step, how long does the voltage across C take to reach 90% of its final value?
questions.explanation:
With the source off (a short), the capacitor sees \(1\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\parallel 4\ \mathrm{k}\Omega=800\ \Omega\).
\(\tau=R_{\mathrm{th}}\cdot C=800\ \Omega\times 2\ \mathrm{nF}=1.6\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). Reaching 90% takes \(t=\tau\ \ln 10=2.303\tau=3.684\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistake: using \(R_{1}+R_{2}=5\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) (a series sum) instead of the parallel combination.

questions.prompt: Preview of slew rate. An op-amp stage that follows an RC filter \((\tau=2\ \mu\mathrm{s})\) can only change its output by at most \(SR=0.5\ \mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s}\). The filter's output has its steepest slope, \(V_{s}/\tau\), right after a step of height \(V_{s}\). What is the largest step \(V_{s}\) that keeps the maximum slope within the slew-rate limit?
questions.explanation:
Maximum slope of the step response: \((dv_{o}/dt)\) at \(t=0^{+}=V_{s}/\tau\). Require \(V_{s}/\tau\le SR\) ⇒ \(V_{s}\le SR\cdot\tau=(0.5\ \mathrm{V}/\mu\mathrm{s})(2\ \mu\mathrm{s})=1\ \mathrm{V}\).
Larger steps force the amplifier into slewing (a straight-line ramp) instead of the clean exponential. Common mistake: using \(\tau\) in the wrong place (\(V_{s}\le SR/\tau\) gives nonsense units).

questions.prompt: Preview of capacitive loading. A common-source amplifier's output node behaves, for small signals, like an RC low-pass with \(R_{o}=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\) driving a load capacitance \(C_{L}=50\ \mathrm{pF}\). After a small input step, how long does the output take to settle to within 1% of its final value?
questions.explanation:
\(\tau=R_{o}\cdot C_{L}=10\ \mathrm{k}\Omega\times 50\ \mathrm{pF}=0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\). Within 1% means \(e^{-t/\tau}=0.01\) ⇒ \(t=\tau\ \ln 100=4.605\tau\).
\(t=4.605\times 0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}=2.303\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
Common mistake: using \(1\tau=0.5\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) (that is the 63% point, not 1% settling).
questions.figure_alt: Normalized step response approaching 1 with a dashed line at 99 percent.

questions.prompt: With the capacitor removed and the independent sources off, the capacitor's node sees \(R_1\) in parallel with \(R_2\). Write that resistance using the names \(R1\) and \(R2\).
questions.explanation: Parallel resistances share the node, so the combination is the product over the sum. Adding \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) is the series total. Using only the source resistor ignores the second path.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth curve, with no resistor values on it.

questions.prompt: A linear circuit starts at rest. An input of 2 V produces 0.8 V at the output node, and a separate input of 3 V produces 1.2 V there. What does an input of 5 V produce at that node?
questions.explanation: Superposition adds the responses of inputs that add: \(0.8+1.2=2.0\ \mathrm{V}\). The 5 V input is the sum of the 2 V and 3 V inputs. Averaging 0.8 and 1.2 drops one of the contributions.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth rising output with no voltage labels.

questions.prompt: A linear circuit's impulse response is a rectangle of height 2 from \(t=0\) to \(t=1\ \mathrm{s}\), and 0 after that. The input is a step of height 3 that starts at \(t=0\). What is the output at \(t=0.5\ \mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation: Convolution with a step that is still on walks over the rectangle that has occurred so far. From 0 to 0.5 s the impulse response is 2 and the input is 3, so the output is \(3\times 2\times 0.5=3\). Using the full 1 s width of the rectangle includes time that has not happened yet.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth curve that is still rising at mid-window.

questions.prompt: The same linear circuit responds to a unit step with the value 4 at a fixed time. By linearity, what does it respond with, at that same time, when the step height is 2.5?
questions.explanation: Linearity scales the whole response by the input height: \(2.5\times 4=10\). Adding 2.5 to 4 treats the step height as a second input instead of a scale factor.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth rising curve with no scale marked.

questions.prompt: A student finds the resistance seen by a capacitor. Exactly one step is wrong.
questions.explanation: The resistance is measured with the independent sources off. A voltage source that stays in the circuit is a short only after it is turned off. Leaving it in holds a node at a fixed voltage and changes the resistance.
steps: Replace each independent voltage source by a short.
Replace each independent current source by an open.
The resistance seen by the capacitor is the resistance of what remains.
Leave a voltage source in place, because it sets the bias the capacitor will reach.
reasons: An independent voltage source is replaced by a short when the resistance is measured. Leaving it in is not that short.
Current sources should be replaced by shorts.
The capacitor stays in the network while its own resistance is measured.

questions.prompt: Which network, from an external input to the labeled output, is linear and time-invariant?
options: Resistors and capacitors only, with fixed values.
The same resistors plus a diode in series with the source.
A resistor and a capacitor whose capacitance is set by a second input.
A switch that changes the resistor at a fixed time after the input arrives.
questions.explanation: Fixed resistors and capacitors obey linear element laws with constant coefficients. A diode is not linear. A capacitance set by another input multiplies two signals. A switch that moves at a set time makes the equation depend on absolute time.
questions.figure_alt: A smooth curve that could be a linear step.

questions.prompt: An impulse response is a rectangle of height 4 from \(t=0\) to \(t=0.2\ \mathrm{s}\). A step input of height 2 starts at \(t=0\). What is the output at \(t=0.1\ \mathrm{s}\)?
questions.explanation: Only the first 0.1 s of the rectangle has been covered. The output is \(2\times 4\times 0.1=0.8\). Using the whole 0.2 s width counts time beyond the instant being asked.
questions.figure_alt: A rising curve over a short window.
